title: ARTICLE ARCHIVE Leadership When a Client Asks for One More Thing
author: Chiarelli, Andrea
summary: Chiarelli opens with a $9M deal loss: a partner answered a late discount request with a lecture on pricing rationale rather than asking what the discount was meant to unlock. The client concluded that if this team could not re-orient in the room, they would struggle across a multi-year programme. This frames a broader argument about adaptability as a professional differentiator. Most people adjust their content under pressure while leaving the same assumptions, tone, and interpretive frame unchanged. True adaptability requires updating the operating system, not just the output -- noticing in real time that the frame you are using has stopped fitting. Chiarelli distinguishes this from agreeableness: the most adaptable professionals have the clearest hypotheses, which is what allows them to re-orient fast. The practical move: acknowledge the ask, ask one clarifying question about what the request is meant to unlock, then respond to what actually helps the client get to yes.
points: - The $9M case shows the cost of answering the wrong question is not just a missed response but a signal about what the engagement at scale would look like -- the room becomes a microcosm of the programme. - True in-the-moment adaptability requires noticing that the frame you are using has stopped fitting, not just updating your words while keeping the same underlying interpretation running. - Adaptable people are not go-with-the-flow types; the fastest re-orienters have the clearest hypotheses about what is happening and the strongest sense of what they are trying to achieve. - The practical pivot move is a single clarifying question that uncovers what the request is meant to unlock, converting a deflection into a collaboration. - We often adjust content while keeping the same internal operating system -- updating every slide but presenting in the tone that was right three months ago, before the relational dynamics in the room changed.
quotes: The question was raised in the last five minutes of our orals presentation, where we had to convince our client we were the right partner for their $9M technology transformation. The procurement lead leaned forward and said, almost conversationally: We liked your approach, but in order for us to move faster we need an additional discount. Can you do that?

He did what a lot of smart, experienced people do when a new variable enters late: he defaulted to expertise. He talked about how the pricing already reflected the maximum discount, how the scope had been carefully considered, how the value justified the rate. He was not wrong, but he was answering a different question to the one that had just been asked.

What the client read between the lines was that the team struggled to re-orient fast. In an informal conversation with the client weeks later, they told us the pricing answer was not really the issue. What had unsettled their team was the sense that if we could not re-orient to a simple late question in the room, we might struggle to do it across a multi-year, complex programme.

Before going further, it is worth retiring a common misreading: that adaptable people are the agreeable, go-with-the-flow types. In serious work, adaptability shows up with backbone. The people who re-orient fastest usually have the clearest hypotheses about what is happening.
We often adjust the content while keeping the same assumptions running underneath every single adjustment. In practice, we often adjust the content while keeping the same internal operating system.
The skill here is noticing, in real time, that the frame you are using has stopped fitting.
